newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Another milestone in the Hong Kong countdown passes.
newsitem.headline: Another milestone in the Hong Kong countdown passes.

text.p: Princess Anne flew into Hong Kong on Tuesday for what is likely to be her last visit to the territory as a British colony, to preside over another little step in the dismantling of the British empire.

She was greeted by Governor Chris Patten at the start of her four-day visit, during which a government spokesman said she will open the new British Consulate Building built in preparation for Hong Kong's handover to China in little more than 150 days from now.
The new building symbolises the changes in store for Britain, which staked its claim to this tiny outpost on China's southern coast more than 150 years ago.

When the red and gold flag of China rises over Hong Kong on July 1, the official British presence in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China will retreat into the consulate, perched on a hillside near the territory's Supreme Court.

The Union flag will no longer fly over Government House, home to the British Governor. Chinese immigration officers will no longer issue British passports. The Hong Kong police will no longer bear a Royal prefix and crowns on their silver buttons.
Instead, the British mission will be just another consulate among dozens clustered in wealthy Hong Kong, gateway to China and springboard for mouthwatering commercial opportunities.
As the countdown gathers pace, the symbols of the British imperial past are fading fast.
Thousands of people queued patiently for hours over the weekend for the first issue of new Hong Kong postage stamps that bear no profile of Anne's mother, Queen Elizabeth.
A week earlier, just as many had turned out in droves to buy up the final issue of stamps bearing the Queen's head.
Anne's visit will probably not be the last by a member of the Royal family before the British set sail from Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, 1997.
That honour falls to her elder brother, heir to the throne, Prince Charles.
Half a century ago, Anne's Great Uncle, Lord Mountbatten, presided over independence for India -- the beginning of the end of the British empire.
Exactly 50 years later, his great nephew Charles will sail in upon the Royal Yacht Britannia for the final curtain call.
A handful of farflung tiny dependent territories scattered across the world still fly the British flag.
Gibraltar. The Caymans. Pitcairn. The Turks and Caicos. But Hong Kong is the last glittering jewel in the crown.
The industriousness of its population of just six million has turned the tiny territory into an economic colossus.

The world's eighth largest trading economy. Holder of the world's seventh largest pool of foreign reserves. Home to Asia's second largest stock market. The world's fifth largest banking centre and foreign exchange market.
As a former British official put it, for China, Hong Kong represents "the largest dowry since Cleopatra".
